reference_title: Design and Construction of Mechanically Stabilized Earth Walls and Reinforced Soil Slopes

sections.title: Top of Wall Elements
sections.body: The top of wall must be addressed from both aesthetic and technical perspectives. Aesthetically, it should provide a smooth profile. Technically, it must integrate roadway elements including pavements, traffic barriers, and drainage features. Top of wall elements include copings, traffic barriers, parapets, post-and-beam barriers, and drainage-related elements.
key_points: Top of wall integrates aesthetic and functional roadway elements
Elements: copings, traffic barriers, parapets, guardrail posts, drainage features
Details shown in this chapter are initial guidance — modify for specific projects and products
sections.applicability: All MSE wall top-of-wall design and detailing.

sections.title: Copings
sections.body: Copings create a smooth, aesthetically pleasing clean line at the top of an MSE wall. Copings may be cast-in-place or precast; precast copings are generally installed more rapidly. Common details for cast-in-place and precast copings are shown in Figures 5-1a through 5-1c for segmental precast concrete facing units, and Figure 5-1d for precast cap units on modular block walls.
key_points: Coping purpose: aesthetic clean line at top of wall
Precast coping: faster installation than cast-in-place
Different details for precast panels (Figures 5-1a to 5-1c) and MBW units (Figure 5-1d)
sections.applicability: Coping details for segmental precast panel and MBW-faced MSE walls.

sections.title: Traffic Barriers
sections.body: Traffic barrier base (moment) slab minimum length is 20 ft (6 m), jointed with shear dowels, width typically 4-6 ft (1.2-1.8 m). Designed per AASHTO (2007). Base slab must prevent overturning and sliding during impact. When the base slab extends over facing unit tops to form a coping, a recess and positive bond breaker (both vertical and horizontal) must be provided to isolate the barrier from facing units and prevent direct impact or prying loads on top panels. If precast coping or traffic barrier is used, the wall top must be smooth and free of steps; level-up concrete fill is cast on facing units to achieve this. Traffic barrier impact loads are addressed in Chapter 7 for extreme event design.
key_points: Base slab: min 20 ft (6 m) long, 4-6 ft (1.2-1.8 m) wide, jointed with shear dowels
Bond breaker (vertical and horizontal) required when slab extends over facing units
Bond breaker isolates barrier from face units — prevents direct impact and prying loads
Precast coping/barrier requires smooth wall top — use level-up concrete fill
sections.applicability: Traffic barrier details for MSE walls supporting vehicular traffic.

sections.title: Parapets
sections.body: Where only pedestrian or bicycle loads are anticipated, a concrete pedestrian parapet (cast-in-place or precast rail directly on top of facing units) may be used instead of a traffic barrier. Parapets use a moment slab (which may also serve as a sidewalk) for stability. The moment slab must be designed to resist the nominal (ultimate) strength of the pedestrian parapet. Where vehicular load is possible, protect the parapet with a non-mountable curb or design it for vehicle impact.
key_points: Parapet: pedestrian/bicycle use only — not designed for vehicular impact
Moment slab provides stability and may serve as sidewalk
If vehicular traffic possible: add non-mountable curb or design parapet for vehicle impact
sections.applicability: Pedestrian parapet details for MSE walls with pedestrian or bicycle loading only.

sections.title: Post and Beam Barriers
sections.body: Guardrail or post-and-beam barrier posts are driven directly into the reinforced soil mass or installed in concrete-filled forms during backfill placement. Post placement requirements: minimum 3 ft (1 m) from wall face, driven 5 ft (1.5 m) below grade. Soil reinforcements should be spaced to miss the posts where possible. If reinforcements cannot be avoided, design the wall to account for the obstruction following procedures in Section 5.4.2.
key_points: Guardrail posts: min 3 ft (1 m) from wall face, embedded 5 ft (1.5 m) below grade
Space reinforcements to miss posts where possible
If obstruction unavoidable: design wall for obstruction per Section 5.4.2
sections.applicability: Guardrail and post-and-beam barrier installation in MSE walls.

sections.title: Drainage Related Top of Wall Elements
sections.body: Top of wall surface should be graded to drain water away from the wall whenever possible. A grassed swale or concrete ditch behind the facing can collect and remove water. When grading away from the wall is not possible, additional drainage details per Section 5.3 must be implemented.
key_points: Grade top of wall surface away from wall face whenever possible
Grassed swale or concrete ditch behind facing to collect and remove water
When cannot drain away: implement Section 5.3 drainage details
sections.applicability: Surface drainage at top of all MSE walls.

sections.title: Bottom of Wall Elements
sections.body: The primary bottom-of-wall element is a leveling pad. Requirements: (1) Use lean (2,500 psi [17.2 MPa]) unreinforced concrete for structural walls — strength and thickness designed to allow cracking during differential settlement; gravel pads only for landscape walls. (2) Common thickness 6 in. (150 mm); width must extend at least 3 in. (75 mm) beyond facing unit thickness. (3) Top of leveling pad within any given step must not vary by more than 1/8 in. (3 mm) over 10 ft (3 m). (4) Openings between steps must be filled after first row of panels: lean concrete for >3 in. (75 mm) openings; geotextile filter for smaller openings. When roadway is immediately adjacent to wall base, a crash protection barrier or non-mountable curb is required to protect against vehicular impact.
key_points: Leveling pad: 6 in. thick lean concrete (2,500 psi); width ≥ facing thickness + 3 in. each side
Structural walls: concrete pad required (not gravel) to control cracking at differential settlement
Top of pad level tolerance: ≤ 1/8 in. (3 mm) in 10 ft (3 m) within each step
Step openings > 3 in. (75 mm): fill with lean concrete; smaller: geotextile filter
Adjacent roadway: crash barrier or non-mountable curb to protect wall base from vehicles
sections.applicability: Leveling pad design and detailing for all MSE walls.

sections.title: Drainage
sections.body: Good drainage is essential to MSE wall performance. Two types: internal (control of surface or subgrade water infiltrating the reinforced soil mass) and external (water flowing externally over or around the wall). Cardinal rule: allow unimpeded water flow through the wall, or collect and remove water before it enters the zone of influence. Key concerns: hydrostatic pressure buildup, piping/erosion, and external soil erosion at toe, edges, and top. Drainage features are recommended for all walls unless specifically determined not required. Effect of fines: soils with less than 3-5% non-plastic fines are free-draining and allow unimpeded flow if reinforced fill permeability > retained fill permeability. When fines exceed 3-5%, permeability drops significantly and drainage features are required to address seepage and hydrostatic buildup. Permeability of fill ≤ approximately 0.002 cm/sec can result in destabilizing seepage forces during severe rainstorms.
key_points: Two drainage types: internal (infiltration into reinforced mass) and external (surface runoff/groundwater)
Goal: unimpeded flow or collect and remove before entering wall zone of influence
Free-draining fill: < 3-5% non-plastic fines; permeability of reinforced fill > retained fill
Fill permeability ≤ 0.002 cm/sec: drainage features required to prevent seepage forces
Drainage required for all walls unless engineer specifically determines otherwise
sections.applicability: Drainage design principles for all MSE walls.

sections.title: Internal Drainage Systems
sections.body: Internal drainage addresses two forms: (a) drainage near the wall face from infiltration of surface water, and (b) drainage behind and under the reinforced soil mass from groundwater. Groundwater may flow from excavation backcuts or rise from beneath the wall. Key internal drainage elements include: chimney drains (vertical or inclined geotextile or granular drains) at the back of the reinforced zone to intercept lateral groundwater flow; base drains (horizontal granular or geocomposite drain at the wall base) to collect and remove water; and drainage blankets. Design requires proper filter criteria to prevent piping and clogging. Perforated pipe with sock or slotted pipe in granular drainage aggregate is the typical internal collection system. Outlets must be provided to discharge collected water at regular intervals (typically not more than 50 ft [15 m] spacing along the wall base). For free-draining reinforced fill, MSE walls may be designed for hydrostatic pressure if drainage features are not provided; basic soil mechanics principles apply to determine effect of phreatic surface on wall loads.
key_points: Two internal drainage forms: near-face infiltration and groundwater behind/below reinforced zone
Chimney drain: vertical or inclined geotextile/granular drain at back of reinforced zone
Base drain: horizontal collection at wall base; outlet pipes at regular intervals (≤ 50 ft)
Filter criteria must be satisfied to prevent piping and clogging
Free-draining fill (< 3-5% fines): drainage system may not be needed but outlet still required
sections.applicability: Internal drainage system design for MSE walls with groundwater or infiltration concerns.

sections.title: External Drainage
sections.body: External drainage deals with water flowing externally over or around the wall. Two categories: (1) intercepting and diverting surface water flowing toward the wall from upslope areas (swales, berms, ditches, curbs); and (2) providing drainage blankets or cutoffs in retained fill zones where groundwater flows from adjacent hillsides or where springs exist. The top of wall surface should be sloped to drain away from the wall. For walls in areas with significant upslope drainage, impervious barriers (geomembrane caps) at the top of the reinforced zone can prevent surface water infiltration. Per Article 11.10.8 AASHTO (2007), when geomembranes are used, a roughened surface PVC, HDPE, or LLDPE geomembrane with minimum thickness of 30 mils (0.75 mm) should be used; geomembrane friction with soil must be checked.
key_points: External drainage: intercept and divert upslope surface water away from wall
Swales, berms, ditches, curbs: divert surface runoff away from wall
Geomembrane cap at top of reinforced zone prevents surface water infiltration
Geomembrane: roughened PVC/HDPE/LLDPE, min 30 mils (0.75 mm) per AASHTO 11.10.8
Check geomembrane frictional resistance against soil — may require reinforcement below
sections.applicability: External surface and groundwater drainage for MSE walls.

sections.title: Filtration and Drainage System Component Requirements
sections.body: Drainage system components must satisfy geotextile filter criteria to prevent piping of finer soils into coarser drainage materials and prevent clogging of drainage materials. Key filter design criteria: (1) Geotextile filter criterion for piping resistance: O95 ≤ D85 of the protected soil (or similar criteria from FHWA NHI-07-092). (2) Permeability criterion: kgeotextile ≥ 10 × ksoil. (3) Clogging criterion: minimum Opening Size (O95) and Gradient Ratio testing per ASTM D5101. (4) Drainage aggregate gradation must satisfy filter criteria with the adjoining soils. (5) Pipe selection: perforated pipe diameter sized for flow; slots/holes not larger than the drainage aggregate. (6) Adjoining sections of geotextile filter/separator must be overlapped by minimum 12-18 in. (300-450 mm) depending on installation conditions. Geocomposite drains with fabric-wrapped cores are an efficient alternative to aggregate drains for tight spaces.
key_points: Filter criterion: geotextile O95 ≤ D85 of protected soil (piping resistance)
Permeability criterion: kgeotextile ≥ 10 × ksoil
Clogging: minimum opening size + gradient ratio testing (ASTM D5101)
Geotextile overlap: minimum 12-18 in. (300-450 mm) at splice joints
Geocomposite drains: efficient alternative to aggregate drains in tight spaces
sections.applicability: Filter and drainage aggregate component design for MSE wall drainage systems.

sections.title: Maintenance of Drainage
sections.body: Drainage features must be maintained over the life of the structure. Pavement cracks above MSE walls should be sealed to prevent water infiltration. Differential settlements and pavement cracks around catch basins should be corrected. Drain pipe outlets require screens to prevent animal nesting and clogging. Outlet screens and cleanouts should be detailed on retaining wall construction drawings. Outlets in soil embankments should drain onto a concrete apron and be marked with a permanent metal fence post to prevent coverage by mowing or subsequent construction. The apron and post should be detailed on wall construction drawings.
key_points: Seal pavement cracks above wall; fix differential settlements and cracks at catch basins
Screens on drain pipe outlets — prevent animal nesting and clogging
Outlet cleanouts detailed on construction drawings for access
Embankment outlets: concrete apron + permanent metal post marker for mower protection
sections.applicability: Long-term maintenance of MSE wall drainage features.

sections.title: Internal Details
sections.body: Internal details address specific design and construction issues within the reinforced soil mass that affect long-term performance. Topics include: dissimilar metal contact, vertical and horizontal obstructions, face penetrations, slip joints, wall curves, corners, and two-stage facing systems.
key_points: Internal details critical to long-term MSE wall performance
Topics: dissimilar metals, obstructions, penetrations, slip joints, curves, corners, two-stage facing
sections.applicability: Internal detailing for all MSE walls.

sections.title: Contact between Dissimilar Metals
sections.body: Galvanic corrosion can occur when dissimilar metals contact each other in the reinforced soil. Therefore, all steel soil reinforcements must be separated from other metallic elements (steel piles, drain pipes, anchor rods, etc.) by at least 3 in. (75 mm). This minimum separation prevents galvanic action and associated accelerated corrosion.
key_points: Dissimilar metals in contact cause galvanic corrosion — accelerates steel reinforcement loss
Minimum 3 in. (75 mm) separation between steel reinforcements and all other metallic elements
Applies to piles, drain pipes, anchor rods, and any other metallic elements in reinforced zone
sections.applicability: All MSE walls with metallic reinforcements near other metallic elements.

sections.title: Vertical Obstructions in Reinforced Soil Mass
sections.body: Vertical obstructions (catch basins, sign foundations, bridge foundations, light poles, culverts) must never be accommodated by cutting, bending, or leaving reinforcements unconnected in the field without approval from the engineer of record. Three design alternatives for unavoidable obstructions: Alternative 1 — Fit reinforcement around obstruction without cutting: splay strip reinforcements up to 15 degrees (reduce capacity by cosine of splay angle); add extra facing connections; use strong back angle across panels; do not splay bar mats >3-5 degrees or cut cross bars. Alternative 2 — Sever reinforcement and provide additional reinforcement in surrounding layers to carry the additional load; design the facing in front of the obstruction for local overturning/sliding stability. Alternative 3 — Install a structural frame (designed per AASHTO Section 6) around the obstruction to transfer loads from facing through frame to reinforcement elements behind the obstruction. Best practice: relocate the obstruction or reinforcement to eliminate interference. Obstructions that apply loads to the wall (e.g., deep foundations, signs, light poles) require additional reinforcement and facing support for local stress increases.
key_points: Never cut, bend, or disconnect reinforcements in field without engineer approval
Alternative 1: Route around obstruction — splay strips ≤ 15° (reduce Tn by cos(splay)); no bar mat splaying
Alternative 2: Sever with increased surrounding reinforcement; design local face stability
Alternative 3: Structural frame around obstruction per AASHTO Section 6
Best practice: relocate obstruction or reinforcement to avoid interference
Load-applying obstructions (piles, signs): design for local stress increase
sections.applicability: MSE walls with vertical obstructions (catch basins, piles, sign posts, etc.) in reinforced zone.

sections.title: Horizontal Obstructions in Reinforced Soil Mass
sections.body: Horizontal obstructions (utilities, storm drain pipes) running along the wall length should be avoided — they create construction problems and can be expensive to repair/maintain. If unavoidable: (1) Inextensible reinforcements may be deflected vertically up to 15 degrees of vertical skew (Figure 5-21) — more than 15 degrees breaks galvanization and reduces tensile/pullout resistance. (2) Geogrids per Figure 5-22. (3) Back-up panels where routing is not possible (Figure 5-23). Never tie reinforcements to pipes. Utility pipes in reinforced fill will settle differentially and should use double-wall systems with inspection galleries or double-wall pipe with leak detection. Only leak-proof joints on drainage pipes. Flexible connections where differential movement is anticipated. Pressurized water mains must not be constructed within an MSE structure.
key_points: Horizontal obstructions (utilities) in reinforced zone should be avoided
Inextensible reinf.: vertical deflection ≤ 15 degrees — more breaks galvanizing
Never tie reinforcements to pipes; never place pressurized water mains in MSE structure
Pipe joints must be leak-proof; flexible connections where differential movement expected
Preferred: double-wall pipe with leak detection for utilities in reinforced zone
sections.applicability: MSE walls with utility pipes or other horizontal obstructions in reinforced zone.

sections.title: Wall Face Penetrations
sections.body: Pipes passing through the wall face must have facing elements designed to fit around the pipe with fill retention and stability. Differential movement between facing and reinforced fill must be anticipated; dry packing around the pipe should be done after the wall is substantially complete. Granular pipe bedding is more permeable than wall fill and can conduct water — a headwall at the end of the pipe prevents water from entering the bedding. Flow paths from pipe bedding/backfill to drainage aggregate must be detailed with filtration criteria addressed; weep holes through concrete face collar may be needed to drain pipe bedding. Catch basins and manholes penetrating through fill may have granular backfill that conducts water — provide drainage if surrounding fill is less permeable.
key_points: Facing designed to retain fill around penetration; dry pack after wall is substantially complete
Granular pipe bedding conducts water — headwall required to block water entry
Flow path from pipe bedding to drainage aggregate must be designed with filter criteria
Weep holes in face collar may be needed to drain pipe bedding
Manhole/catch basin backfill: provide drainage if less permeable than surrounding fill
sections.applicability: MSE walls with pipe penetrations through the wall face.

sections.title: Slip Joints
sections.body: Slip joints are full-height continuous vertical joints allowing independent vertical movement of adjacent wall sections. Used where abrupt differential settlement, wall height changes, or rigid foundation features would otherwise overstress horizontal joints. Conditions meriting slip joints: differential settlement > 1% (0.01); abrupt wall height change ≥ 5 ft; wall underlain by rigid feature (abutment footing, rock outcrop); light rigid structure (box culvert) intersects wall face; wall terminates into cast-in-place structure; tight horizontal curves. Slip joint designs for precast panels use either an exposed slip joint panel with its own reinforcement or a hidden backup panel behind the facing (Figure 5-26). Modular block detail shown in Figure 5-27.
key_points: Slip joint = full-height vertical joint allowing independent section movement
Required when: differential settlement > 1%, height change ≥ 5 ft, rigid foundation features
Also required at CIP structure terminations and tight horizontal curves
Precast panels: exposed slip joint panel or hidden backup panel (Figure 5-26)
Normal panel-to-panel connection is broken at slip joint — fully independent movement
sections.applicability: MSE walls with anticipated differential settlement, height changes, or rigid foundation discontinuities.

sections.title: Wall Curves
sections.body: Curves are approximated by chords equal to the nominal facing unit width. MBW units navigate sharper curves than large precast units. For precast panels: 5 ft (1.5 m) wide units achieve minimum radius ~50 ft (15 m) with 3/4-in. (19 mm) joint opening. For curved walls: provide clear plan details for wall layout relative to roadway alignment, with dimensions for offsets from reference alignments and whether offsets are to top or bottom of wall. For geogrid reinforcement (100% coverage) in curved walls: minimum 3 in. (75 mm) soil layer between overlapping geogrid sections to maintain pullout resistance (geosynthetic-geosynthetic contact has lower friction than soil-geosynthetic). Steel strip reinforcements are discrete and can be placed perpendicular to curved wall face.
key_points: Curves approximated by panel-width chords; smaller units accommodate sharper curves
5 ft precast panels: min radius ~50 ft with 3/4-in. joint opening
Geogrid overlap zones: minimum 3 in. (75 mm) soil between layers to maintain pullout
Clear plan layout required: offsets from reference alignment, top vs. bottom of wall
sections.applicability: MSE walls with horizontal curves.

sections.title: Wall Corners and Two-Stage Facing
sections.body: Wall Corners: When two MSE wall segments form external or internal corners, both segments tend to move laterally outward, causing corners to open. Corner elements must accommodate differential movements, prevent fill from moving through cracks, and provide aesthetic treatment (Figures 5-29a and 5-29b). Acute angle corners (< 70 degrees) should be avoided; if unavoidable, design as a bin wall for the extent where full-length reinforcement cannot be installed, with reinforcement connected to both wall faces or overlapped. Full-height vertical slip joints required at the interface of acute corner and adjacent normal wall sections. Deformation compatibility between the bin wall section and the rest of the MSE structure must be evaluated. Two-Stage Facing: Used where significant differential settlements (> 1/100) are anticipated. Stage 1: flexible wire mesh or geosynthetic face wall constructed with turn-buckle connectors for Stage 2 attachment, then allowed to settle. Stage 2: concrete facing panels installed after settlement is within acceptable limits. Leveling/foundation pad required for Stage 2 with alignment pins or dowels. Detailed structural analysis and design of turn-buckle connectors is required. Construction sequence must be clearly noted on plans.
key_points: Corners open due to outward lateral movement — corner elements required for all corners
Acute corners (< 70°): avoid; if unavoidable, design as bin wall with vertical slip joints
Two-stage facing: Stage 1 flexible face allowed to settle; Stage 2 rigid panels installed after
Two-stage: turn-buckle connectors between Stage 1 wire face and Stage 2 concrete panels
Two-stage suitable for differential settlement > 1/100 where other measures are infeasible
sections.applicability: MSE wall corners and two-stage facing systems for large differential settlements.

sections.title: Wall Initiations and Terminations
sections.body: Junctures of MSE walls with other structures (CIP structures, slopes, existing ground) are critical locations prone to distress including misaligned facing units, backfill leakage, and erosion. Key design recommendations: (1) Juncture with CIP structures: prevent loss of fines and allow differential settlement using bituminous joint filler or backer rod and sealant system (Figures 5-31 for precast panels, Figure 5-32 for MBW units). A CIP structure may have a lip to mask the joint with a geotextile behind the joint to contain soil. (2) Avoid abrupt wall height changes near initiation/termination — causes differential settlement and panel rotation; avoid leveling pad steps within 10 ft (3 m) of wall start/end. (3) At slopes and existing ground: protect against erosion with vegetation and adequate embedment; use riprap with filtration aggregate or geotextile for steep slopes or stream banks; use swales to divert water away from wall ends.
key_points: CIP structure junction: bituminous joint filler or backer rod + sealant; geotextile to retain fill
Avoid abrupt height changes near start/end — no leveling pad steps within 10 ft of wall ends
Slope/ground terminations: protect with vegetation, adequate embedment, riprap for streams
Swales at wall ends to divert water away from termination points
sections.applicability: MSE wall initiation and termination junctions with CIP structures and natural ground.

sections.title: Aesthetics
sections.body: MSE walls readily incorporate aesthetic treatments through precast facing units. Choice of treatments is virtually unlimited, but must be compatible with precasting processes and construction tolerances. Key aesthetic guidelines: (1) Form-liner costs must be included in project estimate — special fabrication, limited reuse. (2) Relief of protruding artwork should be less than 1.5 in. (38 mm). (3) Do not hang heavy treatments from facing unless facing units and reinforcements are designed for the added forces. (4) Consider construction tolerances in form-liner fabrication. (5) Relief patterns between CIP structure and MSE wall are not recommended — interrupt with false column or other feature. (6) Horizontal patterns parallel to panel joints may not align after construction due to differential settlement. (7) Prefer irregular patterns (e.g., Ashlar stone) that hide imperfections at panel joints. (8) Consider sun angle at wall location — sunlight accentuates aesthetic features and imperfections. (9) Select colors compatible with facing material and weathering. (10) Aesthetic treatments using obstructions, acute corners, and face penetrations require careful design review and increased inspection.
key_points: Virtually unlimited aesthetic options for precast facing units — form-liners, exposed aggregate, color
Relief ≤ 1.5 in. (38 mm) for protruding artwork
Do not extend relief patterns across CIP/MSE junctions — interrupt with false column
Irregular patterns (Ashlar stone) hide differential settlement imperfections at joints
Account for sun angle effects — accentuates reliefs and imperfections
Aesthetic treatments with special details (obstructions, penetrations) require extra inspection
sections.applicability: Aesthetic treatment design and guidelines for MSE wall precast facing units.
